title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E297 recasts Euler's 1744 solution of the isoperimetric/variational problem (find y(x) making A = ∫_0^a Z(x,y,p,q,r,...) dx extremal, with p=y', q=y'', r=y''', ...) using Lagrange's δ-algorithm, but derived 'from purely analytical principles'.

Page 106: Because x is not varied (δx=0), the variation of Z is δZ = N δy + P δp + Q δq + R δr + ..., where N, P, Q, R are the partial derivatives of Z with respect to y, p, q, r. Using the commutation δd = dδ proved on the previous pages, δp = (δy)', δq = (δy)'', δr = (δy)'''.

§XX: The variation of the integral is δA = ∫_0^a (N δy + P δy' + Q δy'' + R δy''' + ...) dx. Euler stresses that the variation acts pointwise in x, while the integration runs over x. To avoid mixing the two kinds of 'differential', he renames δy as ω, an arbitrary infinitely small function of x.

§XXI (p.107): He notes that dx is taken constant, so the higher differentials are true derivatives. He then integrates each term by parts repeatedly:
- ∫P ω' dx = Pω − ∫ω P' dx;
- ∫Q ω'' dx = Qω' − Q'ω + ∫ω Q'' dx;
- ∫R ω''' dx = Rω'' − R'ω' + R''ω − ∫ω R''' dx.
Collecting terms gives
δA = ∫ω (N − P' + Q'' − R''' + ...) dx + ω(P − Q' + R'' − ...) + ω'(Q − R' + ...) + ω''(R − ...) + ...

§XXII: The same result is restated with δy in place of ω and extended to S = ∂Z/∂s (s = y''''). This is the general first-variation formula for higher-order Lagrangians: an integrated Euler–Poisson expression plus the boundary terms built from the canonical 'Ostrogradsky-type' momenta.

The next page kills the boundary terms by fixing the endpoint data. It then localizes the variation to obtain N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − ... = 0, which Euler identifies (§XXV) with the equation of his 1744 Methodus inveniendi.
errors: The boundary ('absolute') terms are written only as functions of the upper limit. The contribution at x=0 (or the constant of integration) is left implicit. It is harmless because on the next page the endpoint variations are set to zero, but strictly the bracketed terms should be evaluated as [ ]_0^a.
Arithmetic and signs of all integrations by parts check out correctly.
Minor: the result is valid only with dx constant (uniform parametrization), which Euler explicitly notes.

ideas.what: First variation δZ = NΔy + Pδp + Qδq + ... with δx=0 and δ commuting with d, giving δp=(δy)', δq=(δy)''
ideas.modern_name: First variation / Gateaux derivative of a higher-order Lagrangian; commutation of variation and differentiation
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297 (Novi Comm. 10, 1766); later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Repeated integration by parts separating an integral term containing only δy from boundary terms in δy, δy', δy''
ideas.modern_name: Integration by parts in the first variation; boundary terms with Ostrogradsky-type momenta P − Q' + R'' − ..., Q − R' + ..., R − ...
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange 1760–62; the higher-order canonical formalism to Ostrogradsky (1850)
ideas.where_published: E297; E296; Institutiones calculi integralis III

ideas.what: Euler–Poisson equation N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + ... = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744); name after Poisson

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known textbook derivation of the first-variation formula and the Euler–Poisson equation in Euler's adoption of Lagrange's δ-method. E297 is discussed in standard histories of the calculus of variations (e.g., Goldstine; Fraser). The boundary terms that would give natural boundary conditions are written down but not exploited here; that is also known material.
transcription_corrections: In the image δr is printed as δr = dddδy/dx³ (the transcription's d³δy/dx³ is equivalent).
§XXI: the third integral is printed as ∫dx.Q dd ω/dx² = ∫Q ddω/dx = Q dω/dx − ω dQ/dx + ∫ω ddQ/dx, consistent with the transcription.
